question: A link has `<a href='https://example.com' target='_blank' rel='noopener'>`. Which security vulnerability does rel='noopener' prevent?
options: prevents the new window from accessing window.opener and navigating the original page
prevents the new page from reading cookies from the original domain
prevents cross-origin requests from the new window
prevents the new window from closing the original tab
explanation: Without `rel='noopener'`, the new window retains a reference to `window.opener`, allowing the new page to navigate or manipulate the original window, creating a security risk.

question: A site uses `Download` to link to an image. When clicked, what happens?
options: the image is downloaded to the user's device
the image is displayed in a new page or tab
the browser navigates to the image url like any link
behavior depends on whether the server sends content-disposition header
explanation: An anchor tag navigates to the URL; whether the image is displayed or downloaded depends on the server's Content-Disposition header and the browser's file-handling rules.

question: A link uses `<a href='page.php?id=5&name=test'>`. Why might a database lookup fail?
options: url parameters must be separated by semicolons, not ampersands
php does not parse query strings in href attributes
the ampersand should be escaped as & in html
the php file cannot receive multiple parameters in url
explanation: In HTML, `&` must be escaped as `&` to be valid markup; some parsers may misinterpret unescaped `&` as the start of an entity reference.

question: A page uses `<link rel='canonical' href='https://example.com/page'>` pointing to itself. Why is this redundant?
options: canonical should point to a different version of the page, not itself
canonical links are ignored by search engines when pointing to the same url
search engines already treat the current page as canonical
having any canonical tag makes pointing to self unnecessary
explanation: The canonical link is for indicating the preferred version when duplicate content exists; self-referencing is redundant since the page is inherently canonical.

question:
Why might `Back to Top` not work if the page has no `` or `
`?
options: the anchor fragment is ignored if no matching id or name exists
modern browsers create an implicit top anchor
hash navigation only works for ids, not name attributes
the link will cause a JavaScript error
explanation: Fragment identifiers require a matching element with an `id` attribute or (in older HTML) a `name` attribute; if neither exists, the link is ineffective.

question: A link uses `<a href='http://example.com' download>`. Which file is downloaded?
options: the entire webpage is downloaded as an html file
the resource pointed to by the href is downloaded with its name
the browser prompts for a filename and downloads the resource
download attribute requires a filename, this link is invalid
explanation: The `download` attribute (with or without a value) causes the browser to download the linked resource instead of navigating to it, using the provided name or the resource name.

question: A page has `<link rel='prefetch' href='next-page.html'>`. Why might this not prefetch on slow networks?
options: prefetch requires a minimum bandwidth threshold before fetching
prefetch is a hint, not a guarantee; browsers may ignore it based on connection speed or user settings
prefetch only works for css and js, not html
slow networks require rel='preload' instead
explanation: The `prefetch` directive is a performance hint; browsers may choose not to prefetch on slow connections, low-battery devices, or when data-saving mode is enabled.

question: Why should `<a href='data:text/html,<script>alert(1)</script>' target='_blank'>` be avoided?
options: data: urls are blocked by default in all browsers
data urls with script content execute in the context of the current origin
target=_blank is incompatible with data: urls
data urls are deprecated and will be removed
explanation: Data URLs with HTML/script content execute in the same origin context, potentially creating XSS vulnerabilities if user input is embedded.

question: A site uses `<a href='//cdn.example.com/file.js'>` instead of `https://cdn.example.com/file.js`. What advantage does this provide?
options: protocol-relative urls use http if the page is http, https if the page is https
protocol-relative urls load faster because they skip protocol negotiation
protocol-relative urls bypass the browser cache
there is no advantage; protocol-relative urls are obsolete
explanation: Protocol-relative URLs (starting with `//`) automatically use the same protocol as the current page, allowing http/https compatibility without explicitly specifying the protocol.

question: A navigation link is marked as `<a href='/about' aria-current='page'>`. Which screen reader behavior changes?
options: the link is not announced as clickable; screen readers read it as static text
screen readers announce the link with an indication that it is the current page
the link is visually highlighted to match current page
aria-current only works with role='navigation' parent
explanation: The `aria-current='page'` attribute signals to assistive tech that this link represents the currently viewed page, allowing users to know their location in navigation.
